title: A Painted Room Inside a Mound
text: On 21 March 1972, Japan saw its first full-colour tomb mural. Inside the small Takamatsuzuka mound, built around the late 600s or early 700s, a stone chamber barely 1.1 metres high was painted floor to ceiling: a star chart overhead, the sun and moon, the Azure Dragon, White Tiger and Black Tortoise guarding the directions, and painted groups of men and women on the walls.

source.name: Agency for Cultural Affairs, Japan: Takamatsuzuka Tumulus and Kitora Tumulus

title: Whole Families Buried Beside Their Lord
place: Imdang-Joyeong tombs, Gyeongsan, North Gyeongsang, South Korea
text: The Silla-era cemetery at Imdang-Joyeong holds more than 1,600 graves built in about a century. Ancient DNA from 78 people revealed 13 family groups and some children of cousin marriages. Most chilling: in three cases, parents and their children had been sacrificed together and buried as companions for a tomb owner, the first genetic proof of whole-household sacrifice in Korea.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Ancient genomes reveal an extensive kinship network and endogamy in a Three-Kingdoms period society in Korea

title: A Seaside Cemetery of Newcomers
place: Doigahama site, Hohoku, Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi, Japan
text: The dunes of Doigahama have given up the bones of more than 300 people from Japan's Yayoi period. One young woman, about 149 cm tall and buried around 400 to 360 BCE, had her whole genome read. Roughly 87 percent of her ancestry traced to the Korean Peninsula and only 13 percent to Japan's older Jomon people, a snapshot of migrants reshaping the islands.

source.name: Journal of Human Genetics (PMC): Genetic analysis of a Yayoi individual from the Doigahama site

title: Mummies Smoked Over the Fire
place: Con Co Ngua and other sites, Thanh Hoa, Vietnam
text: Hunter-gatherers across southern China and Southeast Asia buried their dead tightly crouched, some folded so hard no flesh could have remained. Testing bones from 11 sites in China, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines, researchers found most had been heated, probably by smoke-drying bodies over fires for long periods. Some of these mummies may be older than Chile's Chinchorro mummies and Egypt's.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Earliest evidence of smoke-dried mummification more than 10,000 years ago in southern China and Southeast Asia

title: A Harappan Couple Facing Each Other
text: Among 62 graves in one part of the Rakhigarhi cemetery, only one held two people: a man and a woman, both young adults, laid on their backs with the man's head turned toward her. Red pots surrounded them and a banded agate bead lay at her collarbone. Researchers think they died at about the same time and found no sign of widow sacrifice.

source.name: Anatomy & Cell Biology (PMC): A young couple's grave found in the Rakhigarhi cemetery of the Harappan Civilization

title: Buried Alongside Their Animals in Kashmir
place: Burzahom, Srinagar, Jammu and Kashmir, India
text: Burzahom, named after the Kashmiri word for birch, was home to people from around 2900 BCE. Its Neolithic and megalithic layers held ten human burials, some rubbed with red ochre, and some skulls even show trepanation, holes cut into the living head. Unusually, animals were laid in the graves beside the people. DNA shows contacts with the Swat Valley to the west.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Ancient mitogenomes from Neolithic, megalithic and medieval burials of the Kashmir valley

title: A Young Prince in Tuva's Valley of Kings
place: Chinge-Tey I, Turan-Uyuk Basin, Tuva, Russia
text: Four metres beneath a huge stone platform in Tuva's 'Valley of the Kings' lay a man of 20 to 25 with gold ornaments, a finely decorated weapon, a long robe and a glass bowl probably made in distant Assyria. His gold work is so like that of the nearby Arzhan-2 queen that the same craftsman may have made both.

source.name: BMC Genomics (PMC): Ancient DNA analysis of an elite nomadic warrior from the Chinge-Tey I complex

title: The Near East's Oldest Funeral Pyre
place: Beisamoun, Hula Valley, Upper Galilee, Israel
text: Beside the ancient Hula Lake, Neolithic villagers dug a plastered pit that worked like a kiln, stacked it with wood and reeds, and burned a young adult seated inside. It is the earliest directly dated intentional cremation in the Near East. The dead person had once survived an attack: a flint arrow tip was still lodged in their shoulder blade.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Emergence of corpse cremation during the Pre-Pottery Neolithic of the Southern Levant

title: Graves Under the Floors at Göbeklitepe
text: For decades Göbeklitepe's giant carved pillars had no intact graves to go with them. Then two turned up beneath plaster floors near the special buildings. One held a single young adult curled on the left side facing east. The other was a family-style tomb where earlier skeletons had been pushed aside for newcomers, their skulls gathered neatly in one corner.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): First burials give insights into mortuary rites at Göbeklitepe

title: Reading DNA From Egyptian Mummies
text: Mummies from the Middle Egyptian town of Abusir el-Meleq, now kept in Tübingen and Berlin, gave up 90 complete mitochondrial genomes spanning 1,800 years. The ancient townspeople were closer to Near Eastern and Levantine peoples than modern Egyptians are, and their genes barely changed under Greek and Roman rule. Most sub-Saharan ancestry arrived in the last 2,000 years.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Ancient Egyptian mummy genomes suggest an increase of Sub-Saharan African ancestry in post-Roman periods

title: Hearing a Mummified Priest Speak
text: Nesyamun chanted and sang the daily liturgy as a priest and scribe at Karnak under Ramesses XI. His coffin calls him 'true of voice'. In 2016 his mummy, now in Leeds, was CT-scanned, and his throat was 3D-printed. Fed by an artificial larynx, it produced a single vowel-like sound somewhere between the vowels in English 'bed' and 'bad'.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Synthesis of a Vocal Sound from the 3,000 year old Mummy, Nesyamun 'True of Voice'

title: Tattooed Toddlers of Christian Nubia
text: Naturally dried bodies from Kulubnarti's cemeteries still carry ink. Using multispectral cameras, researchers found tattoos on at least one in five people, men and women, often a diamond of four dots on the forehead. The youngest was only 18 months old. The marks may be the region's earliest Christian tattoos, or a remedy for fevers and headaches.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Revealing tattoo traditions in ancient Nubia through multispectral imaging

title: Three Graves on Beechey Island
text: Sir John Franklin's 128 men spent their first Arctic winter at Beechey Island, where three crewmen died and were buried in the frozen ground. They were the lucky ones to get graves: not one of the expedition survived. Later tests of bone, hair and tissue found high lead levels, and scientists still debate how much poisoning hastened the disaster.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Franklin expedition lead exposure: new insights from high resolution confocal x-ray fluorescence imaging

title: The Frozen Boy of El Plomo
place: Cerro El Plomo, near Santiago, Chile
text: In 1954 treasure hunters found an eight-year-old boy seated at 5,400 metres on Cerro El Plomo, hugging his knees, frozen for about five centuries. He was an Inca capacocha offering. Long thought to have died quietly of cold, he was re-examined with CT scans and skin studies, which revealed a forceful blow to his skull at the time of death.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Pilgrimage to sacrifice: the Western Andean Capacocha

source2.name: JAAD Case Reports (PMC): Dermatoscopic findings of Niño del Plomo, an Incan mummy in Chile

title: Coca Leaves on a 6,739-Metre Summit
text: Near the top of Llullaillaco, 6,739 metres up, three frozen Inca children were found in 1999. Their hair worked like a diary: the 13-year-old 'Maiden' began taking far more coca about a year before her death, and alcohol peaked in her final weeks. She still had a wad of coca between her teeth, sitting cross-legged with her headdress undisturbed.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Archaeological, radiological, and biological evidence offer insight into Inca child sacrifice

title: A Traveller Melts Out of a Glacier
text: In 1999 a young man's frozen body, still wearing a robe, emerged from a glacier in northwest British Columbia, more than 100 km inland. Named Kwäday Dän Ts'ìnchí, he lived sometime between about 1670 and 1850. His bones showed a life spent eating seafood, but hair and tissue revealed that in his final year his diet switched to inland foods.

source.name: American Antiquity (Cambridge): Radiocarbon Dating and Dietary Stable Isotope Analysis of Kwaday Dän Ts'inchí

title: The Little Angels of Palermo
text: The Capuchin Catacombs hold 163 mummified children, many from middle- and upper-class families. Bodies were dried in a draining room, washed with vinegar and dressed, sometimes injected with preservatives such as arsenic. X-rays of 43 'angioletti', or little angels, revealed hidden metal wires, wooden boards and canes used to shape and pose them for display, plus growth lines showing childhood illness or hunger.

source.name: Frontiers in Medicine (PMC): The 'angioletti' of Palermo: mummified non-adults in late modern Palermo, Sicily (1787-1880 CE)

title: Leprosy in a Bronze Age Round Tomb
place: Dahwa, near Saham, North Batinah, Oman
text: At Dahwa, a Bronze Age trading village near Oman's Batinah coast, the dead were placed in circular Umm an-Nar tombs and their bones later jumbled together in pits. Micro-CT scans of three upper jaws revealed the tell-tale bone loss of lepromatous leprosy. It is the first Bronze Age leprosy found outside South Asia, hinting the disease travelled along ancient trade routes.

source.name: Frontiers in Medicine (PMC): Lepromatous leprosy in Bronze Age Oman: micro-CT in fragmentary and commingled assemblages

title: Mummies in Painted Plaster Shrouds
text: In late Roman Egypt, wealthy families at Saqqara wrapped their dead in stucco shrouds painted with portraits, garlands and other motifs. Two such mummies joined the Dresden collection of Augustus II, King of Poland, in 1728. CT scans found a young woman's brain still in place, necklace beads, a hairpin, lead seals, nails and two coins or medallions hidden inside the wrappings.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Decorated bodies for eternal life: late Roman Period stucco-shrouded portrait mummies from Saqqara

title: The Ancient One's Genome Speaks
text: In 1996 a skeleton about 9,000 years old turned up in Washington state. Skull measurements led scientists to claim he was closer to the Ainu or Polynesians than to Native Americans, and courts blocked tribes from reburying the man they called the Ancient One. His genome, read in 2015, proved otherwise: he was closest to Native Americans, including the Colville tribe.

source.name: Nature (PMC): The ancestry and affiliations of Kennewick Man

title: Strep Throat From a Bolivian Mummy
place: National Museum of Archaeology (MUNARQ), La Paz, Bolivia
text: A naturally mummified person who lived in Bolivia around 1300 CE still had the germ that causes strep throat in one tooth. Scientists rebuilt almost the whole genome of this Streptococcus pyogenes, very like modern sore-throat strains. It shows the bacterium was already circulating among Indigenous Americans before European contact, pushing its confirmed presence in the Americas back by several centuries.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): An ancient genome of Streptococcus pyogenes from a pre-Columbian Bolivian mummy

title: Teak Coffins on Stilts in the Caves
place: Log Coffin caves, Pang Mapha, Mae Hong Son, Thailand
text: In the hills of northwest Thailand, Iron Age people carved huge coffins from single teak trees and raised them on stilts inside more than 40 caves and rock shelters, between 2,300 and 1,000 years ago. DNA from 33 of the dead shows a large, well-connected community. Relatives were often laid to rest in the same cave, so kinship shaped who joined whom.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Genomic portrait and relatedness patterns of the Iron Age Log Coffin culture in northwestern Thailand

title: Chiefs and Commoners in Tongan Mounds
text: At 'Atele on Tongatapu, two burial mounds hold the dead of the Tongan maritime chiefdom, one probably for commoners and one likely for the chiefly class. Chemical traces in their bones show the two groups ate differently, and women ate less protein-rich food than men. Only one of 30 people tested grew up elsewhere, a sign of tight control over who reached the sacred island.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Assessing human diet and movement in the Tongan maritime chiefdom using isotopic analyses

title: Ancestors Found During Roadworks
place: Waikato region, North Island, New Zealand
text: Roadworks in New Zealand's Waikato uncovered seven Māori tūpuna, or ancestors, reburied together in an old borrow pit in the 1700s. Scientists studied chemical traces and proteins in their teeth and bones. All seven lived mostly on plant foods like kūmara and taro, and two local children had been weaned onto plants by age two or three, proof of how central gardens were.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Horticultural intensification and plant-based diets of 18th century CE Waikato Māori

title: Sealed for Eternity With Sticky Rice
text: Song and Ming Chinese families sealed coffins inside a shell of lime, yellow clay, sand and sticky rice water that set like rock. Packed clothing, moisture-absorbing charcoal and germ-killing lime did the rest. A woman buried in De'an in 1274, 152 cm tall, emerged in excellent condition, and such mummies still held the eggs of the intestinal worms that once plagued them.

source.name: BioMed Research International (PMC): Mummification in Korea and China: Mawangdui, Song, Ming and Joseon Dynasty Mummies
